in_text_mentions: Facial weakness, along with other characteristic features of DM1, can contribute to an appearance that may seem tired or expressionless. The facial signs vary from subtle, sometimes only acknowledged as sign of the disease after a patient is diagnosed, to severe myopathic facies. Typical features include bilateral ptosis, difficulty closing the eyes completely, and frontal balding in men. Temporal wasting gives rise to a long, thin facial contour (Fig. 1) [12].

panels.rationale: This is a single H&E histology image of a biceps brachii muscle biopsy from a human patient with myotonic dystrophy type 1, as confirmed by the article title and caption. It shows characteristic disease-specific histologic findings including centralized myofiber nuclei, making it a valid real-patient image of the target disease manifestation.
panels.attribution_text: Sugie et al. Characteristic MRI Findings of upper Limb Muscle Involvement in Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1.. PloS one 2015. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0125051. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Histopathological findings of a biopsy specimen of the left biceps brachii muscle (patient 7 in Table 1). Histopathological examination of a biopsy specimen showed characteristic pathological findings, including central nuclei, variable ranges of fiber size, and fatty degeneration. H&E stain, Bar = 30 μm.
in_text_mentions: The correlations between the muscle MRI findings and the histopathological findings of biopsy specimens of the muscle were examined in patients 4, 7, and 15. In patients 7 and 15, T1-weighted high-intensity signals on MRI of the biceps muscle were associated with characteristic pathological findings, such as central nuclei, variable ranges of fiber size, and fatty degeneration (Fig 4). In contrast, the biceps muscle in patient 4, associated with no high-intensity signals on MRI, showed mild pathological findings without fatty degeneration (data not shown).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Axial head MRI from the reported myotonic dystrophy type 1 case demonstrates frontotemporal cerebral atrophy and severe bilateral temporalis muscle atrophy, indicated by arrows. B: Axial MRI shows the cerebral atrophy described in the caption in a human patient with myotonic dystrophy type 1. C: Coronal MRI demonstrates bilateral temporalis muscle wasting with cerebral frontotemporal and limbic atrophy in the reported myotonic dystrophy type 1 case. D: Axial MRI demonstrates the cerebral atrophy described in the figure caption from a human myotonic dystrophy type 1 case. E: Axial MRI shows the described cerebral atrophy in a human patient with myotonic dystrophy type 1. F: Axial MRI shows the captioned temporal-pole white-matter FLAIR hyperintensity marked by the arrowhead, a recognized MRI manifestation of myotonic dystrophy type 1, with temporalis wasting also visible.

panels.rationale: Single axial brain MRI from a human patient with myotonic dystrophy type 1; the image and caption show bilateral temporal-lobe white matter hyperintense lesions, a recognized MRI manifestation of DM1, in a disease-focused case report.
panels.attribution_text: Rollnik et al. Myotonic dystrophy type 1 presenting with stroke-like episodes: a case report.. BMC research notes 2013. doi:10.1186/1756-0500-6-243. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: White matter lesions were also found in the temporal lobes.
in_text_mentions: Cranial computertomography showed numerous periventricular hypodense lesions without signs of acute cerebral infarction. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed twice revealing general brain atrophy and multiple white matter lesions in all cerebral lobes, including the temporal region (Figures 1 and 2). No gadolinium enhancement and no abnormalities in diffusion weighted images (DWI) were found. No progression of the white matter lesions was detected from June to October on MRI scans.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Real patient T1-weighted muscle MRI in a 51-year-old with genetically confirmed DM1 (CTG 650). Panels show diffuse skeletal-muscle fatty change; in-text documents ankle dorsiflexor (anterior compartment) and finger-flexor weakness, supporting selective anterior-compartment atrophy on MRI. Article title states adult-onset DM1. [raw subtype: adult-onset] B: Serial T1-weighted muscle MRI (5 years after panel A) in the same adult DM1 patient (CTG 650); increased fatty replacement with prominently worsened ankle dorsiflexor weakness. Numeric muscle-score overlays are present. [raw subtype: adult-onset] C: Real patient T1-weighted muscle MRI in an adult with DM1 (patient B, CTG repeat 150) showing skeletal-muscle fatty change. At this initial time point the in-text documents only finger-flexor weakness (grade 3), so the anterior-compartment vocabulary key is not asserted; the visible manifestation is early DM1 muscle involvement on MRI....

Patient B is a 56-year-old woman diagnosed with DM1 5 years previously, with an increased CTG repeat length of 150. panels.rationale: Human T2-weighted cerebral MRI in a myotonic dystrophy type 1 case report. Confluent white matter lesions involving all cerebral lobes including the temporal region support the vocabulary finding for DM1-associated anterior temporal white matter hyperintensity. Generalized brain atrophy is clearly present but not in the supplied vocabulary, so it is proposed. The image is real, readable, and not a diagram, control, or other-disease panel.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 8 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H). A: Axial FLAIR MRI shows pontine and subcortical signal alterations consistent with DM1 white matter disease. B: Coronal T2 MRI demonstrates bilateral anterior temporal white matter hyperintensities, a hallmark finding in DM1. C: Axial DWI MRI shows pontine hyperintensity consistent with T2 shine-through from demyelination. D: Axial ADC MRI shows no hypointense signal in the pons, ruling out acute infarction and supporting T2 shine-through. E: Axial FLAIR MRI demonstrates multiple white matter hyperintensities in cerebellar and subcortical regions. F: Axial FLAIR MRI shows additional white matter hyperintensities in the temporal region. G: Sagittal T2 MRI of the cervical spine included in the radiological demonstration; arrowhead points to upper spinal region. H: Axial MRI highlights muscular atrophy in the lower extremity consistent with DM1 myopathy.

panels.figure_caption: Demonstration of radiological findings in the patient, diagnosed with myotonic dystrophy type 1, utilizing various acquisition techniques. A) fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), axial view; B) coronal T2-weigthed image; C) axial view, diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (DWI); D) axial view, apparent diffusion coeffizient (ADC); E) and F) fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), axial views; G) T2-weigthed image, saggital view; H) T2-weigthed image, axial view with highlighted sign of muscular atrophy. Arrowheads are implemented to highlight pathologies exemplary. The participant provided an informed consent to publish health data including imaging data.
in_text_mentions: Severe dysphagia with aspiration of saliva was identified by FEES. An MRI from the referring hospital already had shown subcortical and pontine signal alterations (Fig. 1). Polygraphy showed a bradypneic episode, lasting 2 hours and 36 minutes with a minimum breathing frequency of 3/minute (Fig. 2) and episodes of ataxic breathing with irregular variability of breathing effort and timing. The in parallel performed trancutaneous canpnography over a period of 10,3 hours revealed a minimum pCO2 of 45 mmHg, median of 52 mmHg, maximum of 61 mmHg with 9 events of a pCO2 > 50 mmHg of a duration of mo

to 800 CTG-repeats. The MRI of our patient revealed pontine signal alterations in FLAIR, T2 and DWI weighted images, while the ADC weighted images showed no hypointense signal in the pontine region (Fig. 1). The elevated signal in DWI weighted images is thus a T2 shine-through and might be explained by demyelination. There is no sign of an acute infarction. This, again, fits well with the neuropathology of DM1, of which demyelination is a key feature [5].
